title: Officer defends arrest of alcoholic woman; Fatality inquiry looking into jail cell suicide
article: The officer who arrested Eva Marion Farnel for being drunk in a public place, just hours before she committed suicide in a police holding cell, testified on Monday he'd do the same thing in the same situation.
"I could not live with myself if we . . . walked away," Const. David Bailey told the deceased's family lawyer, Murray Stone, at a fatality inquiry into the 53-year-old woman's death.
"I saw the apartment and there was no way I'd leave her there to choke. . . . In my opinion, it was abuse if I left her there."
Bailey said he was aware when he arrived at Farnel's residence on 57th Street S.W. at 4:30 a.m. on May 8, 2006, it was the second police visit to the home for a noise complaint in two hours.

He said he initially arrested Farnel for breaching the public peace under the Criminal Code. But after he and other officers escorted the resistant woman from her home, he did her a favour by opting to charge her with the lesser offence of public intoxication under the Gaming and Liquor Act, the city officer said.
Court records show she had blood-alcohol readings of up to .26 at 10:27 a.m., an hour after she was found hanging by her shirt from a metal pipe in a cell at the downtown arrest processing unit.
She succumbed to the self-inflicted injuries four days later.

Earlier Monday, Joyce Stevens, the victim's sister, testified that Farnel was a longtime alcoholic. She was depressed because she was unemployed and in an "unhappy" relationship leading up to the day she hanged herself, Stevens said.
Although Farnel had battled the bottle for 20 years, there was no history of suicide in the family, and she had never spoken of killing herself, the sister testified.
"She resisted our (four siblings') encouragement to do something about her alcohol problem," Stevens said.

"At some family things, she was definitely out of control. She wasn't working, and getting some financial support -- begrudgingly - - from her common-law . . . she was worried about not being employed."
Apartment manager Tom Crawford told court he called police after twice having to go to the second-floor suite because of complaints from neighbours, and was met by a verbally abusive Farnel.
Her abuse continued when she was taken to the downtown police station and eventually placed in the women's drunk tank, homicide Det. Chris Matthews testified.

Less than four hours later, about 9:15 a.m., Farnel can be seen in surveillance video crawling across the floor of her cell. She takes off her shirt, ties it around a pipe near the toilet and hangs herself.
Although there were monitors at the front desk, nobody was watching, court heard.
Matthews said Farnel had been checked by medical staff when first booked, then had her necklace and any other possessions deemed potentially harmful removed from her.

She was checked out by medical staff, who were assured she would not harm herself, then was placed into the cell with a 22-year-old woman. It was after the cellmate was released that the fatal incident occurred.
